clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive sterol-storage disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ABCG5 or ABCG8, encoding the heterodimeric sterolin transporter that effluxes plant sterols from enterocytes and hepatocytes.

Hallmark is markedly increased intestinal absorption and reduced biliary excretion of dietary plant sterols (sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol) and shellfish sterols, with raised plasma phytosterols.
Tendon and tuberous xanthomata may appear in childhood, sometimes with normal or only modestly raised total cholesterol, an important clue distinguishing it from familial hypercholesterolaemia.
Premature atherosclerosis and early coronary events can occur, occasionally in the absence of substantial hypercholesterolaemia.
Haematological features are characteristic: haemolysis with stomatocytosis, macrothrombocytopenia and abnormal large platelets, sometimes mislabelled as immune thrombocytopenia.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating grossly elevated plasma plant sterols by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry, confirmed by ABCG5/ABCG8 genetic testing.

Treatment combines a diet low in plant and shellfish sterols with a cholesterol-absorption inhibitor and bile-acid sequestrants; statins are relatively ineffective because cholesterol synthesis is already suppressed.
Consider the diagnosis in any child with xanthomata plus unexplained haemolysis or thrombocytopenia, and in statin-unresponsive apparent familial hypercholesterolaemia.
reference.pathophysiology: Sitosterolaemia results from biallelic inactivating variants in either ABCG5 or ABCG8, the two half-transporters that assemble into an obligate heterodimer (sterolin) on the apical membrane of enterocytes and the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes. Normally this pump limits absorption of non-cholesterol sterols and promotes their biliary secretion, so that plant sterols are almost entirely excluded from the body. When the transporter is defective, dietary phytosterols and shellfish-derived sterols are absorbed largely unchecked and are poorly excreted in bile, accumulating in plasma and tissues. Feedback suppression of endogenous cholesterol synthesis lowers activity of the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway, which is why circulating cholesterol may be only modestly raised and why statins offer limited benefit. Deposition of sterols in tendons and skin produces xanthomata, while incorporation of abnormal sterols into arterial walls accelerates atherosclerosis. Enrichment of red-cell and platelet membranes with plant sterols alters membrane fluidity and structure, causing haemolysis with stomatocytes and the production of abnormally large, fragile platelets, giving the distinctive haematological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Immune thrombocytopenia or other causes of macrothrombocytopenia
Hereditary stomatocytosis and other membrane haemolytic anaemias
Xanthomata secondary to cholestatic liver disease
additionalInvestigations: Plasma plant sterol quantification (sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol) by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry
ABCG5 and ABCG8 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
Full lipid profile including LDL and lipoprotein subfractions
Full blood count with blood film for stomatocytes, macrothrombocytopenia and haemolysis
Haemolysis screen (reticulocytes, bilirubin, haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase)
Cardiovascular assessment including lipid-focused imaging or coronary evaluation where indicated
Family screening and cascade genetic testing of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Chest pain or other symptoms of premature coronary disease, including in children and young adults
Aortic valve involvement or signs of significant arterial disease at a young age
Severe haemolysis or bleeding from profound thrombocytopenia
Xanthomata unresponsive to statin therapy suggesting an alternative sterol disorder
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, a sterol-restricted diet and cholesterol-absorption blockade, plasma phytosterols fall, xanthomata regress and haematological abnormalities improve, greatly reducing cardiovascular risk. Undiagnosed disease carries a risk of premature, sometimes fatal, atherosclerotic events.
pitfalls: Mislabelling as familial hypercholesterolaemia and relying on statins, which are largely ineffective in this condition
Overlooking the diagnosis when total cholesterol is normal or only mildly elevated despite prominent xanthomata
Attributing the thrombocytopenia and haemolysis to immune or primary haematological disease and missing the underlying sterol disorder
Failing to measure plasma plant sterols because they are not part of a routine lipid panel
Not screening family members, delaying diagnosis in affected relatives
references: Clinical biochemistry and metabolic medicine references
management: Strict dietary restriction of plant sterols and shellfish sterols, avoiding vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and shellfish, as the cornerstone of treatment
Ezetimibe, an intestinal sterol-absorption inhibitor, as the principal pharmacological therapy to reduce phytosterol absorption
Bile acid sequestrants such as colestyramine as adjunctive sterol-lowering therapy, recognising that statins are of limited value because endogenous cholesterol synthesis is already suppressed
Monitoring of plasma plant sterol levels, lipid profile and regression of xanthomata to guide therapy
Management of the haematological features of haemolysis and macrothrombocytopenia, which improve with sterol lowering, avoiding misdirected immune therapy or splenectomy
Cardiovascular risk assessment and surveillance for premature atherosclerosis
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive ABCG5 or ABCG8 disorder
